stances.claim: FIRST: Under Ko v. Republic (April 12, 2023), Family-Code children conceived or born during a marriage are presumed legitimate even when conceived/born during parental separation and biologically the offspring of the wife with a man other than her legal husband. Legitimacy is the civil status established for a person born during the subsistence of a marriage; filiation is the state of being someone's offspring as determined by biology and biotechnology. The biological father cannot petition to tag the offspring as his 'natural child' (which would deprive the child of legitimacy rights including inheritance from the legal father). Only the child (and in some instances the legal father or his heirs) can challenge directly -- not collaterally. 'Even the mother is prohibited by law from declaring against the child's legitimacy.'

SECOND: Under Republic v. Pryce (March 8, 2023), the 20% senior discount 'necessarily include interment services, such as diggings for the deceased person's grave, its concreting, and other services being done during the actual burial.'

THIRD: Under Ong v. Senate (March 28, 2023, Pharmally), congressional legislative-investigation power has four limitations: (1) 'in aid of legislation'; (2) per published rules; (3) rights of appearing persons respected; (4) contempt-based detention only until termination of inquiry. The Senate met the first two but failed the third by citing petitioners in contempt and ordering arrest 'without giving them the opportunity to be heard.' Only detention -- not criminal/civil liability -- was decided.

FOURTH: Under Soliman v. People (April 25, 2023), the Cybercrime Law penalty for online libel is one degree higher than RPC traditional libel; for online libel, courts 'may impose the alternative penalty of fine instead of imprisonment.'

FIFTH: Under 4E Steel Builders v. Maybank Philippines (March 13, 2023), foreign banks may foreclose and acquire mortgaged real property under three conditions: 5-year max possession; no title transfer; required transfer to qualified Philippine national within 5 years.

SIXTH: Under ACT Teachers v. Duterte (January 24, 2023), livestream video and photographs demonstrating absence of a House quorum cannot prevail over the Congressional Journal -- because 'no less than the Constitution itself grants the Congressional Journal its imprimatur.' CJ's added 'humble opinion': separation of powers grants the three branches autonomy on internal processes -- SC respects Congressional Journal entries; Congress respects internal SC deliberations and votes; both respect Executive Cabinet processes.

SEVENTH: Under People v. Almayda (June 14, 2023), in warrantless drug seizures the physical inventory and photo-taking 'must, as a rule, be done in the place of seizure.' Exception at nearest police station/office only when 'clear, consistent, and sensible affidavits' show impracticability or that 'items seized are threatened by immediate or extreme danger.'

one_paragraph_summary: After reviewing the significant 2023 SC decisions, CJ shares seven 'little-known ones' affecting both lawyers and ordinary people. FIRST, under Ko v. Republic (April 12, 2023), Family-Code children conceived or born during a marriage are presumed legitimate even when conceived/born during parental separation and biologically the offspring of the wife and a man other than her legal husband. The Court distinguished legitimacy ('the civil status established for a person born during the subsistence of a marriage') from filiation ('the state of being someone's offspring as determined by biology and biotechnology'). The biological father cannot petition to tag the offspring as his 'natural child' because that would deprive the child of legitimacy rights including inheritance from the legal father. Only the child (and in some instances the legal father or his heirs) can challenge directly -- not collaterally -- because the presumption is for the child's benefit, and 'Even the mother is prohibited by law from declaring against the child's legitimacy.' SECOND, under Republic v. Pryce (March 8, 2023), the 20% senior discount 'necessarily include interment services, such as diggings for the deceased person's grave, its concreting, and other services being done during the actual burial.' THIRD, under Ong v. Senate (March 28, 2023), congressional legislative-investigation power has four limitations: (1) inquiry 'in aid of legislation,' (2) per chamber's published rules, (3) rights of appearing persons respected, (4) contempt-based detention only until termination of inquiry. The Senate (in the Pharmally case) met the first two but failed the third by citing petitioners in contempt and ordering arrest 'without giving them the opportunity to be heard'; only detention -- not criminal/civil liability -- was decided. FOURTH, under Soliman v. People (April 25, 2023), the Cybercrime Law penalty for online libel is one degree higher than RPC traditional libel (prision correcional minimum-medium OR fine P40,000-P1,200,000, or both); for online libel, courts 'may impose the alternative penalty of fine instead of imprisonment.' FIFTH, under 4E Steel Builders v. Maybank Philippines (March 13, 2023), foreign banks may foreclose and acquire mortgaged real property under three conditions: 5-year maximum possession; title not transferred to the foreign bank; required transfer to a qualified Philippine national within the 5-year period. SIXTH, under ACT Teachers v. Duterte (January 24, 2023), livestream video and photographs demonstrating absence of a House quorum cannot prevail over the Congressional Journal because 'no less than the Constitution itself grants the Congressional Journal its imprimatur.' CJ adds his 'humble opinion' that the principle of separation of powers grants the three branches autonomy on internal processes -- SC respects Congressional Journal entries; Congress respects internal SC deliberations and votes; both respect Executive Branch's internal Cabinet processes. SEVENTH, under People v. Almayda (June 14, 2023), in warrantless seizures of illegal drugs the physical inventory and photo-taking 'must, as a rule, be done in the place of seizure.' The exception -- at the nearest police station or apprehending officer's office -- applies only when 'clear, consistent, and sensible affidavits' show (1) impracticability of place-of-seizure inventory or (2) seized items threatened by 'immediate or extreme danger' at the place of seizure.
